html:
The Kingdom of Scotland held the northern third of Great Britain and its islands from the 800s until it joined England in 1707. The map shows it from 1000 to 1700.

It grew out of a union of the Picts and the Gaelic Scots, traditionally under Kenneth MacAlpin around 843; the result was called Alba. Later kings took in the Britons of Strathclyde and English-speaking Lothian. David I, in the 1100s, founded towns and abbeys on English and French models.

The defining struggle was with England:

  • In 1296 Edward I of England invaded and took the crown.
  • William Wallace and then Robert the Bruce fought back, and Bruce won at Bannockburn in 1314.
  • The nobles' Declaration of Arbroath of 1320 asked the pope to recognise Scotland's freedom.
  • The Auld Alliance with France lasted for centuries; James IV died fighting the English at Flodden in 1513.

The Reformation came in 1560, led by John Knox, and made Scotland Presbyterian. In 1603 James VI inherited England's throne in the Union of the Crowns, but the two kingdoms kept separate parliaments and churches. After the costly failure of the Darien scheme, a Scottish colony in Panama, the Acts of Union of 1707 merged Scotland into Great Britain, the state of England, then Britain.
sum: The Kingdom of Scotland held the northern third of Great Britain and its islands from the 800s until it joined England in 1707. The map shows it from 1000 to 1700.
